Adverserial Networks (GANs) can be used to create synthetic data with similar characteristics to real-world data when it comes to both tabular data and images.  Despite the differing data types, the core structure of the GAN model remains unchanged, leading to the suggestion that the theory behind GAN's should be universally applicable.  However, little research has been done exploring how GANs truly generate data, largely due to difficulties in visualizing the complex processes involved. By comparing data from CMS and STAR on pion, kaon, and proton asymcarries, we observe a consistent pattern where the largest asymcarries occur when projecting onto directions most likely associated with pions produced closest to the point of collision.  A similar pattern holds true for proton and kaon asymcarries, despite their generally lower levels of anisotropy.  Utilizing a multi-component model, we attribute the observed pattern to competition between positive pions from decay of $\Lambda$'s and negative pions from decay of kaons, as well as the minimal contribution of proton anisotropy to overall charge asymmetry.  Furthermore, we find that hadron charge asymcarries in $p\bar{p}$ collisions correlate inversely with those in 200 GeV two-body relativistic collisions of $\Lambda$ and $\bar{\Lambda}$, contradicting previous speculation but aligning with theoretical predictions.  As a result, we can exclude any significant influence of $B$-meson decays on charge asymcarries and reject the possibility of significant nonperturbative gluon effects in low transverse momentum regions.  Ultimately, we confirm that charge asymcarries in $p\bar{p}$ collisions primarily result from decay of hadrons produced closest to the point of collision, with little to no contribution from nonperturbative gluon effects.  This research has implications for possible measurements of $\Lambda$ and $\bar{\Lambda}$ charge asymcarries in future high-energy hadron collisions. subject of axion models has have continued to evolve in response to emerging patterns in physics, particularly those observed in the spectrum of particle physics. As the standard model of physics fails to account for certain characteristics observed in certain particles, new ideas and theories have been introduced to fill the gaps. At low energy levels, axions remain a viable option, as they are capable of resolving the problem of CP symmetry non-conservation and contributing to the universe's dark matter. Furthermore, with the discovery of heavy, quenching particles that participate in the strong interaction, a new compartment has been added to the spectrum of low-energy particles, which can be filled by the axion or its related phenomena. Moreover, as the axion's properties are closely tied to the underlying physics of the universe's earliest moments, its study also provides valuable insights into the universe's formation and evolution. In this article, we explore the possible relationships between axion models and emerging patterns in physics, with a focus on the latest research findings. As the majority of the underlying physics is dedicated to the strong interaction, we prioritize non-standard, top-down approaches to axion models, which are distinct from established, bottom-up models. Furthermore, we delimit our scope to the Earliest Universe Hypotheses that Underlie the Formation of Large-Scale Structures, Allowing for a Minimal Description of Dark Matter's Cold Behavior. Lastly, we outline the key characteristics that viable axion models should aim to meet, including our current understanding of its properties, as well as the most effective search methods for detecting axions or its related phenomena. Ultimately, as the development of axion models is inextricably linked with our understanding of the universe's earliest moments and its evolution, its study also provides valuable insights into the universe's formation and its current state.  The text of this article consists of three main sections, each focusing on a distinct area of research: (I) new patterns in physics that the standard model of physics fails to account for; (II) non-standard approaches to axion models; (III) the possible relationship between axion models and the Earliest Universe Hypotheses that Underlie the Formation of Large-Scale Structures. Additionally, we have included three separate appendices, which provide a detailed description of missing information mentioned in the article, along with a list of open questions in the field of axion models for readers to consider. We present a comprehensive proof system for verifying  concurrent programs that exhibit a wide range of behaviors, including  systems with unbounded buffers, tree-like data structures, and programs  that release resources.  Our proof system consists of five basic rules and  three verification conditions, which can be mechanically verified using  a prover such as Levi or Sledge.  We demonstrated the effectiveness of our  proof system by creating 20 verified programs across various categories,  including programs that utilize a variety of data structures and algorithms,  as well as programs that use locks and condition variables to manage access  to shared resources.  We also applied our proof system to three substantial  case studies: (1) a port of the Linux socket implementation that handles  socket backlogs, (2) a version of the Linux socket implementation that  handles socket time-wait buffers, and (3) a popular free real-time  operating system's socket buffer management program.  All of the verified  programs and case studies have been made available for download at an  associated repository.  We further conducted a performance evaluation of  our proof system by automating the verification of our programs using  Levi, which resulted in end-to-end verification times of less than 30 seconds  for all programs and case studies.  We believe that our proof system can  serve as a foundation for developing verified concurrent programs at a  large-scale level.  We also contributed to the theoretical development by  establishing two fairness unwinding theorems, which can be utilized in  the verification of programs that employ unbounded recursion under weak  fairness assumptions.  We made our research available in the form of  three separate papers, which can be found at an associated repository.  The first paper presents the proof system along with its verification conditions  and the performance evaluation.  The second paper delves into the  theoretical development of our fairness unwinding theorems.  The third  paper provides an in-depth description of our approach to verifying weak  fairness assumptions.  We also included three appendices that provide  additional information on our research, which includes a tutorial on how  to create verified programs using our proof system, a list of frequently  asked questions, and a description of how our research contributes to the  broader context of concurrent program verification. The most stringent limits on the decay constant of an axion, focusing on decay frequencies between $10^{9}$ and $10^{12}$ eV, are as follows:  an axion decay frequency less than 10$^{10}$ eV results in a decay constant less than 10$^{-3}$ eV;  an axion decay frequency less than 10$^{11}$ eV results in a decay constant less than 10$^{-2}$ eV;  an axion decay frequency less than 10$^{12}$ eV results in a decay constant less than 10$^{-1}$ eV;  an axion decay frequency of approximately 9.66 GHz results in a decay constant of less than 10$^{-6}$ eV;  an axion decay frequency of approximately 23.5 GHz results in a decay constant of less than 3.5 x 10$^{-6}$

We analyzed large-scale molecular dynamics by comparing observations from the APERO survey and the HI21CM ASSEMBLE survey, as well as theoretical models presented in a companion study (Paper I).  Results. We found that giant molecular fluctuations move at approximately 20 km/s, which is significantly faster than the velocity of tidal density waves proposed by a bar-driven torque model (around 10 km/s).  Conclusion. Our findings suggest that the primary driver of giant molecular fluctuations is likely not a bar-driven torque, but rather the gravitational instability of the galaxy's disk.  This is also in agreement with the results from Paper I, which showed that the amplitude of these fluctuations cannot be explained by a tidal wave model.  As a result, we propose an alternative model where giant molecular fluctuations are driven by the gravitational instability of the galaxy's disk, influenced by the presence of spiral arms and the dispersion of supersonic molecular flows.  This new model is also consistent with the results presented in Paper II, which explored the relationship between giant molecular fluctuations and star-forming regions.  This research contributes to our understanding of the relationships between giant molecular fluctuations, star formation, and galaxy evolution, and provides a new perspective on the dynamics of large-scale molecular dynamics in star-forming galaxies.  Based on the findings, we propose a revised framework for understanding the relationship between giant molecular fluctuations and star formation, which prioritizes the role of the instability of molecular flows over the influence of tidal waves. algorithm, dubbed Perceptive Arithmetic Coding (PAC), that leverages the predictive information of the context-based entropy coding scheme, typically part of arithmetic coding systems, to encode binary data efficiently.  Initially, a first-order Markov model is applied to calculate initial codewords; the context-based entropy coding scheme then uses a history of recent symbols to predict the next symbol's probability.  To counter the increased computational requirements of a more complex context-based scheme following a poor prediction, the algorithm uses a simpler scheme such as unary encoding.  Implemented in hardware to evaluate the proposal, a context-free scheme with 32 contexts, along with an architecture for the hardware, yielded performance data for various binary data types including images, videos, music, and compression standards. interested in using image features extracted from videos for navigation and mapping, given the significant advancements in drone technology and the decreasing cost of high-definition cameras.  Although significant progress has been made in 2D feature mapping, the potential for drones to fly in complex indoor environments is limited due to the scattering of wireless signals, making wireless signals a crucial factor for navigating and mapping areas that are hard to access.  As a result, researchers are exploring the use of wireless signals that curve and diffuse in intricate ways in tight spaces, such as molecules of light in art installations, pharmaceuticals, and even certain types of cancer.  To create accurate maps of these light-carrying structures, researchers are evaluating the possibility of combining 2D feature maps derived from video frames with the characteristics of wireless signals in tight spaces.  To determine the feasibility of this approach, the paper investigates the connection between the accuracy of 3D reconstruction and the resilience of image features to the changing patterns of wireless signals in various contexts.  In one example, phosphorescent art installations that glow for several hours after illumination are discussed, and in another, the paper examines the possibility of using image features to map the distribution of light that penetrates the layers of cancer tumors.  The paper investigates the stability of Steinhardt features, a strong and resilient image feature extraction method, in response to the oscillations of wireless signals in tight spaces, as well as other difficult situations, and analyzes the possibility of using 3D reconstruction to measure the depth of light-carrying structures by conducting experiments with museum art installations, pharmaceuticals, and computer simulations.  The results show that Steinhardt features exhibit excellent resilience to the changing patterns of wireless signals in various contexts, outperforming other strong feature extraction methods, and that 3D reconstruction can be effectively used to measure the depth of light-carrying structures by conducting experiments with museum art installations, pharmaceuticals, and computer simulations.  The research findings provide a scientific framework for exploring the possibility of combining 3D reconstruction and the characteristics of wireless signals in tight spaces, and the paper offers a proposal for a feasible name for this line of inquiry, Wireless Signal-Based 3D Reconstruction, and suggests that phosphorescent art installations, pharmaceuticals, and certain types of cancer are suitable subjects for this approach.  The paper contributes to the development of a new area of research that has the potential to make significant contributions to various fields, and as a representative study, it offers a set of open questions for further investigation. Using a high-energy laser to create a pair of particles in the cavity, the system's non-equilibrium behavior can be initiated. nearly simultaneous collisions involving three particles in a three-body interaction process are distinguished concepts.  Sequential collisions occur when one particle interacts with another, then quickly interacts with a third particle, whereas nearly simultaneous collisions take place when three particles interact with each other nearly at the same time.  Utilizing leading-order QCD and a specific choice of parton distribution functions, we analyze nearly simultaneous and sequential three-body particle interactions in central pseudorapidity regions with 7 TeV proton-proton collisions.  With nearly $10^5$ observed events, we examine nearly simultaneous and sequential three-body particle interactions through $K^+\Lambda$ and $\Lambda\bar{\Lambda}$ final states.  Our research finds that nearly simultaneous three-body particle interactions are predominantly $strange$maquarks, whereas sequential interactions are mostly $baryon$ic.  This distinction holds true for both $K^+\Lambda$ and $\Lambda\bar{\Lambda}$ final states.  Additionally, our data indicates that nearly simultaneous three-body particle interactions through $K^+\Lambda$ and $\Lambda\bar{\Lambda}$ final states are scarce, with less than 20 observed events for each state in nearly $10^5$ observed events.  However, as we explore different transverse momentum thresholds, we find that nearly simultaneous three-body particle interactions through $K^+\Lambda$ and $\Lambda\bar{\Lambda}$ final states become more prevalent.  Furthermore, our research discovers that nearly simultaneous three-body particle interactions through $K^+\Lambda$ and $\Lambda\bar{\Lambda}$ final states occur more frequently when higher transverse momentum thresholds are applied.  Moreover, as transverse momentum thresholds decrease, nearly simultaneous three-body particle interactions through $K^+\Lambda$ and $\Lambda\bar{\Lambda}$ final states become more likely in proportion to sequential interactions.  This findings align with theoretical predictions that three-body particle interactions are predominantly strange and occur nearly simultaneously.  This research contributes to our understanding of strange three-body particle interactions in proton-proton collisions and offers insights for future studies. One fundamental protein property is the free energy landscape, which governs movement and interaction behavior. Despite its significance, calculating the free energy landscape of proteins remains a significant challenge. In the current study, we introduce a novel integrated molecular dynamics and metadynamics simulation approach called "beta-NEAT" to accurately compute the free energy landscape of proteins at the atomic level. This approach builds on the native-enhanced potential (NEAT) method but adds a harmonic bias to stabilize native state conformation, thereby significantly improving native state representation and description. Additionally, we developed a automated script to calculate and embed hydrogen atoms in protein systems between simulations, which is critical for accurate description of hydrogen bonding in protein systems. We applied the beta-NEAT approach to three challenging protein systems: ubiquitin, a 64-kilodalton HIV-1 protease drug target, and a designed protein called "protein L." We obtained precise free energy landscapes for all three systems with minimal computational expense, which we further validated through multiple simulation repetitions and comparison with alternative methods. We believe that the beta-NEAT approach has the potential to revolutionize protein protein free energy landscape calculation by eliminating the need for ambiguous resolution cuts and biases, thereby enabling accurate description of low probability native-like conformations. Furthermore, we observed that the free energy landscape of protein L exhibits a distinct minimum at a specific conformation that closely matches the experimentally determined structure, demonstrating the approach's capability to calculate the free energy landscape of designed proteins. Finally, we applied the beta-NEAT approach in combination with traditional protein design methods to design a new protein with a targeted free energy landscape, which we called "protein Q." We successfully designed a protein with a free energy landscape that matches the desired characteristics, confirming the approach's viability for de novo protein design. We anticipate that the beta-NEAT approach will be highly valuable for protein protein design, understanding protein function, and understanding protein evolution.  (Figure Not Available). Through the use of quantum mechanics, we have performed a comprehensive analysis of the quantum behavior of LSPR in metal nanoparticles, focusing on silver and gold nanoparticles in air.  By doing so, we have overcome the limitation of the classical model in describing LSPR and its properties.  Our quantum mechanical research shows that LSPR exhibits oscillatory and decaying characteristics, with the decay a manifestation of energy loss and particle dissipation. Despite the difficulty, we can develop a numerical index to represent a society's moral character by analyzing how people behave in uncertain or unpredictable situations, where choices are not influenced by self-interest.  This approach is inspired by classic thought experiments in ethics, such as the trolley problem, and allows us to prioritize values by ranking them in a linear order.  This order serves as a metric to evaluate a society's moral stature, with more important values receiving higher scores.  To calculate this index, we conduct surveys among members of a society to determine the preferred actions in various scenarios, then plot these preferences on a graph to determine the most valuable action in each scenario.  Once we have a list of the most valuable actions, we can assign a point value to each one based on its position in the list, with the most valuable action worth the most points.  We can then calculate the average point value of all the actions in each scenario to obtain a numerical value representing the society's willingness to act with integrity in that situation.  This value is our measure of the society's moral character in that scenario.  To ensure our index is a valid representation of a society's values, we must demonstrate that it is consistent, scalable, and insensitive to trivial variations in behavior.  Additionally, the index should reflect the inherent properties of the scenarios, such as the difference between actively causing harm and passively allowing it to occur, and the absence of bias against certain groups of people.  We can also test the index by comparing the values of scenarios that are known to be morally equivalent and those that are known to be inversely related.  Furthermore, the index should correlate with other established measures of moral character, such as people's self-reported values and behaviors.  To further validate the index, we can conduct surveys among members of different societies with varying cultural backgrounds to determine if their values align with universally accepted moral principles.  If the index accurately reflects a society's values, it should prioritize actions that promote the well-being of its members and condemn those that harm them, even if the actions involve personal sacrifice.  The index should also distinguish between actions that are right in themselves and those that are right because they lead to good outcomes.  Finally, the index should be capable of distinguishing between scenarios that are similar but not identical, such as the difference between pushing a large person in front of a trolley and pushing a small person in front of a trolley.

climate dynamics, affecting both the planet's energy balance and cloud formation.  As a result, accurate predictions of aerosol particle concentrations are crucial for climate modeling.  Although aerosol quantities can impact the formation of clouds and thus influence the amount of solar energy reached at the Earth's surface, current global forecasting systems exclude this feedback effect when predicting aerosol particle concentrations.  To address this limitation, researchers have explored the possibility of incorporating aerosol feedback into forecasting models, which is a complex task due to the intricate relationships between aerosols, clouds, and energy balance.  To evaluate the feasibility of including aerosol feedback in forecasting models, researchers have simulated such a scenario using large computational networks, which allows for the examination of the effects of aerosol feedback on forecasting accuracy in different regions of the world and in various seasons.  The results of these simulations indicate that incorporating aerosol feedback into forecasting models does not significantly improve their accuracy for most regions and seasons, likely due to the high precision required to detect subtle changes in aerosol quantities that influence the formation of clouds.  However, in areas affected by massive aerosol events, such as forest fires or volcanic eruptions, including aerosol feedback into forecasting models can lead to better predictions of aerosol concentrations and the formation of clouds.  Furthermore, these simulations reveal that aerosol feedback has a minimal impact on the overall energy balance in the atmosphere, likely due to the high frequency of weather forecasts, which often struggle to accurately predict cloud formation even without considering aerosol feedback.  Nevertheless, in regions impacted by massive aerosol events, the product of forecasting models that incorporate aerosol feedback and traditional models can provide more accurate indicators of the formation of clouds than either model alone, which is valuable for evaluating the overall health of the atmosphere even if it contradicts the product of other forecasting models.  To further explore the potential benefits of incorporating aerosol feedback into forecasting models, researchers have examined the effects of massive aerosol events, such as forest fires and volcanic eruptions, on the formation of clouds and the energy balance in the atmosphere, which can aid in developing more effective evaluation methods.  For instance, in the case of a massive volcanic eruption in Iceland in 2010, which spewed large amounts of ash into the atmosphere, affecting European weather patterns, a product of forecasting models that incorporated aerosol feedback and a traditional model showed a higher correlation with observed cloud formation in Europe than either model alone, which is valuable for evaluating the impact of such events on the formation of clouds and the energy balance in the atmosphere

, particularly in 5G systems, managing and optimizing network performance has become increasingly complex. As a result, there's a growing need for efficient methods to control and direct network traffic at this stage. In this paper, we present a novel idea for an intelligent, self-organizing network framework that prioritizes critical traffic over less urgent data through the use of variable reward signals. This framework, coupled with a simple actor-critic learning algorithm, allows for efficient control over traffic prioritization at a minimal computational cost. Using realistic scenarios based on real-time 5G network data, we demonstrated the effectiveness of this intelligent framework in maximizing critical data throughput and reducing delay, while also withstanding variations in data arrival patterns and the presence of external noise. Furthermore, our results indicate that this intelligent framework can be seamlessly integrated with various resource allocation strategies and techniques, paving the way for its application in various 5G network scenarios. Ultimately, our findings confirm that by simply adjusting the reward value, we can achieve a fair balance between throughput and edge computing costs in edge-fanout video streaming, a previously unachievable feat with conventional methods.  This research paves the way for using learning-based techniques to optimize complex 5G network decision-making processes.  With its focus on a specific, real-world problem and its realistic scenario-based evaluations, this study offers a practical blueprint for implementing such techniques in real 5G network environments.  Additionally, due to its novel variable reward strategy, we believe that our framework can be applied to a wide range of similar 5G network scenarios and industry areas, including multimedia big data services, massive MIMO systems, and millimeter wave systems.  Furthermore, the code for this research is available online, allowing others to build upon our findings.  As the 5G network is set to transition to a more sustainable 6G technology, we anticipate that this research will serve as a foundation for the development of new, environmentally friendly, and high-performance network strategies. Since the fundamental connection between galaxies and their halos is reflected in this relationship, accurately predicting it is crucial.  However, due to limitations in resolving small scales, current simulations are not sufficient for determining the galaxy-halo relationship, particularly for low-mass galaxies.  To overcome these limitations, theoretical models of the galaxy-halo relationship have been developed, with a goal of incorporating it into large-scale structure predictions.  Despite the importance of the relationship, its precise simulation is not necessary for its theoretical formulation.  Instead, as demonstrated in previous studies, a simple self-consistent model that accounts for the conditional bias in transforming the halo mass distribution into the galaxy distribution can be effective.  Building on these findings, we propose a straightforward, analytical model of the galaxy-halo relationship, which aligns with theoretical expectations.  This model can be used to generate mock galaxy distributions for investigating the consistency of simulation results on large scales, as well as providing a useful tool for conducting similar analyses within the $N$-body dark matter simulation suite presented in a companion paper. We examine the scenario in which the cosmos became structured through a non-linear growth of fluctuations, with the linear growth only accounting for large scales.  We investigate the conditions necessary for the second order perturbation theory to apply to the curvature perturbations in such a scenario, focusing on single field inflation models.  We also explore the parameters that meet these conditions, analyzing the relationship between the scale of the structure and the model's characteristics.  We observe that a minimum value of $\nu \geq 0.1$ is required for the non-Gaussianity to be negligible, with a maximum amplitude of $10^{-5}$ for structures on a scale of $10^{16}$m.  We further note that more massive structures demand a higher value of $\nu$, with a maximum value of $10^{-3}$ for structures on a scale of $10^{25}$m.  We discuss the implications of these findings on the formation of large structure on megaparsec scales, as well as the possibility of the universe experiencing a sudden acceleration in its expansion.  We also explore the possibility of certain structures forming through a combination of the linear growth of fluctuations and the non-linear growth of curvature perturbations, with the latter contributing significantly on scales of $10^{20}$m.  We emphasize that this study focuses on the development of structure through the non-linear growth of curvature perturbations, with little consideration given to the formation of anisotropies in the cosmic microwave background or the large scale structure of the universe.  We note that a more sophisticated approach is necessary to calculate the non-Gaussian features of the perturbation distribution on the largest scales, as well as the formation of structures through the non-linear growth of perturbations in other contexts, such as the formation of structures in the universe's late stages and the development of structure in certain multi-field inflation models.  We additionally highlight the importance of studying the non-linear growth of curvature perturbations in different inflationary model scenarios, as well as the need for further research into the formation of structure on the largest scales through other theoretical approaches, such as the formation of structure through the non-linear growth of perturbations in the universe's early stages and the formation of structure through the non-linear growth of anisotropies in the cosmic microwave background. nanosecond-scale wireless communication technologies have vast applications in high-speed, short-range connections.  To effectively utilize these technologies, accurate real-time location information is necessary.  As users often carry devices that feature both mmWave and Bluetooth capabilities, harnessing the simultaneous use of these technologies may help resolve this issue.  A precise indoor localization system using a mixed mmWave and Bluetooth network is presented in this paper.  The system utilizes triangular positioning based on mmWave signal strength and a walking direction estimator to provide real-time location information.  To further enhance performance, a learning-based approach that trains a neural network on Bluetooth beacons' characteristics is applied to eliminate beacon calibration requirements.  A simulation using a large-scale, 3D indoor model and real-world measurements demonstrates the effectiveness of the system.  The results show that the system can achieve accurate localization even with a limited number of Bluetooth beacons and produces better outcomes compared to individual mmWave and Bluetooth systems.  The study also finds that the system's performance is not significantly impacted by beacon orientation, and as walking direction is accounted for, areas with low mmWave signal strength do not affect localization accuracy.  The proposed system achieves an average localization error of less than 0.5 meters in areas with strong mmWave signals and opens up possibilities for various practical applications.  One potential use is the creation of large, open-area venues for sports and entertainment, and another is the design of complex, multi-level buildings for shopping and culture.  The paper also explores the practical implications of the system's performance metrics, demonstrating that it meets the requirements for various applications.  For instance, with an error margin of 10%, the system can accommodate areas measuring up to 50 meters in length, 20 meters in width, and 5 meters in height.  Furthermore, the system can produce accurate localization information for users moving at speeds of up to 2 meters per second and takes around 20 milliseconds to calculate a single location point.  The study's findings also suggest that the system's effectiveness is not compromised by user carrying different devices with varying Bluetooth capabilities and can accommodate a large number of users within a single area. We explore the stability of localized solutions, known as solitons, in $\mathcal{PT}$-symmetric nonlinear Schrödinger equations with a spatial variation of nonlinearity. Analyzing the stability, we identify two possible instability scenarios: an exponential growth of perturbations at a specific point within the nonlinear region and a diffusion-induced instability at the boundary of the nonlinear area. Additionally, we investigate how the $A$-laméndre operator's properties affect the stability, finding that only the component of the instability wave relevant to the $A$-sector contributes to the diffusion-induced instability. This restriction is crucial for understanding the stability in systems with complex, non-symmetric nonlinear profiles. We further analyze a specific example of an $\mathcal{PT}$-symmetric Kerr media system, which exhibits both types of instability for a particular parameter configuration. Furthermore, we investigate how the stability of solitons relates to other physical properties, including the energy and topological characteristics, finding a direct correlation between the diffusion-induced instability and the topological charge of the soliton. Moreover, we observe that, in systems with a non-uniform nonlinearity profile, the most stable soliton type has the lowest energy. On the other hand, in systems with a uniform nonlinearity profile, the most stable soliton type has the highest nonlinearity level. models in computer vision have exhibited impressive performance in various tasks such as classification, detection, and segmentation. This paper introduces the concept of near-optimal strategies for managing trade-offs in multi-task models, focusing on a prevalent scenario involving classification, detection, and segmentation in computer vision. This research paves the way for optimizing performance in individual tasks by exploring the possibility of approaching ideal boundaries in a margin of at least 10\% in a representative dataset, and further shows that a strong normal distribution contributes significantly to achieving ideal boundaries over an extensive range of values.  Additionally, we include a set of empirical studies illustrating the applicability of our findings to real-world scenarios.  This research is anticipated to contribute significantly to the development of near-optimal strategies for managing trade-offs in multi-task models, as well as other similar models in computer vision and beyond. While deep learning-based methods have significantly improved disparity estimation from light fields, especially in outdoor scenes, they struggle when faced with complex indoor environments and multi-view videos. Given the significance of detecting squeezed states, accurate methods for their identification are crucial.  Typically, operators associated with squeezed states are analyzed, which can be complicated to measure, especially in experiments.  A widely accepted approach to verifying squeezed states involves measuring the spectrum of the output light's quadrature, which requires sophisticated equipment and techniques.  However, a fundamental question remains: what are the basic signatures of squeezed states that can be recognized through straightforward measurements?  In a recent study, it was found that a simple, non-optical way to signify squeezed states exists, involving typical values of variables that represent the core properties of light.  A critical examination of this phenomenon is necessary, which involves analyzing the characteristics of squeezed states, identifying their basic signatures, and exploring their relationship with the phase space of light.  A thorough understanding of these features will provide a solid foundation for recognizing and possibly even generating squeezed states in various situations.  This dissertation aims to thoroughly explore and define the fundamental indicators of squeezed states, which will have implications for both theoretical research and practical applications.  To begin, we review the fundamental concepts of quantum optics, focusing on squeezed states, their characteristics, and key measurement approaches.  A critical examination of the characteristics of squeezed states is then presented, exploring distinctive features that can be recognized through basic optical measurements.  Additionally, we investigate specific scenarios that generate squeezed states, including optical processes and quantum systems, with a focus on identifying distinctive signature patterns.  A comprehensive analysis of the phase space of light is also conducted, exploring how different phases relate to various characteristics of squeezed states.  To further explore distinctive features, we examine various models of squeezed states in detail, focusing on coherent, single-photon, and bound-states models.  A summary of the research findings is provided, followed by a discussion on the implications of the discovered patterns for generating and detecting squeezed states.  Finally, we explore possible future research directions, focusing on generating and detecting squeezed states in various situations, including optical processes, quantum systems, and phase-space characteristics.  In conclusion, this dissertation contributes significantly to the understanding of squeezed states, which is a fundamental concept in quantum optics, with far-reaching implications for both theoretical research and practical applications.  As a notable achievement, this research has led to the discovery of a novel way to produce truly non-local correlated states through the interaction of two quantum systems, which has theoretical implications for both mechanics and optics, and practical applications in quantum communication.

Utilizing this protocol, we derive a practical method for calculating the unknown state's key properties, including its energy and any relevant correlations.  This method is not only theoretically valuable but also offers promising applications in experimental scenarios, as it provides a clear, realistic approach to accessing unknown quantum states without the need for complicated many-body calculations.  To demonstrate the protocol's efficacy, we apply it to a specific, physically motivated example, consisting of a bosonic system separated into two parts, with one part already known and the other unknown.  By applying the proposed protocol in sequence with another, we successfully recover the unknown state's essential characteristics, including its energy and any long-range correlations, through a straightforward, two-step procedure.  This example serves as a concrete illustration of the protocol's capabilities, as it achieves precise results even in scenarios with demanding conditions.  In the case of a harmonic oscillator split into two parts, with one part already known and the other unknown, the proposed protocol delivers an accurate description of the unknown state's key properties by producing a precise, normalized description of the unknown state's characteristics. As a further illustration, for an oscillator of mass m and frequency omega, with one part having a mass of 100 times that of the other, the proposed protocol yields an unknown state's energy of approximately 0.26*omega, in contrast to just 0.17*omega through a straightforward calculation. As a result, there is a growing interest in research on image data, and a crucial aspect of this process is effectively utilizing the data to train models.  Although massive data sets are available, collecting relevant data is a time-consuming process, and the current strategy of using large data sets with a broad variety of samples may not always be optimal.  The goal of this research is to investigate whether the proportion of certain specific images in a data set has a direct impact on how models behave when confronted with similar, previously unseen images.  To achieve this objective, we conducted three distinct experiments with different neural network models, each focused on a unique type of image data (mnist, gmm, and real-world vehicles).  In each experiment, we created two large data sets with a significant difference in the ratio of representative images, and then evaluated how the presence of such images affects both the accuracy and the bias of models.  The outcomes of these experiments revealed that, regardless of the model or data type, a higher presence of representative images in a data set always leads to better accuracy and a decrease in bias.  Furthermore, we observed that even very small proportions of representative images can have a significant effect on both factors.  Additionally, we discovered that the effectiveness of more complex features decreases with a higher presence of representative images, and vice versa, which demonstrates a direct inverse proportionality.  To further analyze these findings, we calculated the information gain of models in relation to the presence of representative images, and the results confirmed our previous observations.  As the presence of representative images can influence both the accuracy and the bias of models, we proposed a simple data obfuscation method to directly measure this impact.  Finally, we demonstrated that the presence of representative images is a critical factor in the phenomenon of bias towards representative images being succeeded by bias towards more complex features.  The findings of these experiments contribute to our understanding of how the presence of representative images affects the behavior of models, and as a result, we propose several practical implications for utilizing the research on image data.  As models are known to prefer images that are similar to representative ones, data providers should strive to include a wide variety of such images in data sets to achieve better outcomes. This model, called the Neural Network Boundary Value Solver, employs neural networks to find an approximate solution to the associated harmonic function, and then uses this solution to construct an adjoined function that satisfies the boundary condition.  Our initial findings indicate that this solver can efficiently find exact solutions to various Klein--Gordon equation boundary value problems, as well as nearly exact solutions when the initial conditions are only partially known. This research investigates a cooperative EH wireless network where multiple nodes share a single receiver for transmission, and the key performance measure is the network's throughput.  Our study utilizes a general model that includes popular schemes such as AF, DF, and relay-chaining, and we derive the throughput boundary for each scheme.  Building on these boundaries, we determine the maximum overall throughput and the optimal transmission strategy for the network.  Our findings demonstrate that in the simplest two-node configuration, the maximum overall throughput is achieved when both nodes transmit immediately, and we confirm popular results from prior studies.  Extending our analysis to more complex scenarios, we observe that for any given number of nodes, the maximum overall throughput is approximately 1 bit per channel use for infinite buffer sizes.  As the number of nodes increases, we establish that the average overall throughput approaches 1 bit per channel use through two distinct paths:  a sequence of cooperative transmissions and a sequence of EH periods.  Furthermore, we discover that for any given number of nodes and time slots, there exists an optimal distribution of time slots between EH periods and communications, and we outline a strategy for achieving the maximum overall throughput.  In the case of an infinite number of nodes, we derive a closed-form formula for the overall throughput.  Finally, we explore the potential for growth in overall throughput as the number of nodes increases, and we demonstrate that it grows linearly with square root of the average signal power for a fixed time slot duration and linearly with the average signal power for a fixed signal-to-noise ratio.  As the number of nodes increases to infinity, we establish that the average overall throughput approaches 1 bit per channel use through both sequences of cooperative transmissions and EH periods.  Additionally, we investigate a scenario with multiple receivers and derive the throughput boundary for a cooperative EH wireless network with three nodes and one receiver.  Our research provides comprehensive insights into the throughput potential of cooperative EH wireless networks and offers strategic guidance for optimizing overall throughput.  The research contributes to our knowledge of EH wireless communication systems by establishing fundamental throughput boundaries for cooperative EH wireless networks, and we believe that it has the potential to influence the design of future EH wireless communication systems.  The paper includes three key findings that can be utilized by system designers to optimize the overall throughput of EH wireless communication systems. However, this theory falls short in explaining why some macroscopic superpositions remain coherent, as seen in quantum interference experiments with large objects like light beams and macroscopic coherent superpositions of small bosonic systems like phonons and microwave fields.  The environment-based approach to decoherence might not be sufficient in accounting for this distinction, prompting an investigation into the microscopic origins of decoherence and its relation to classicality.  We examine the fundamental processes contributing to decoherence in large bosonic systems and find that the environment's decohering effect is not the primary factor in forming classicality.  Instead, decoherence in large systems is primarily a result of quantum fluctuations within the system itself, leading to distinct appearances in closures of the decoherence hierarchy.  This distinct closure pattern holds the key to understanding why some superpositions remain coherent, allowing for a revised definition of classicality that aligns with quantum realism and obedience to the Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen criterion.  This revised perspective on decoherence and classicality is found to be incompatible with the many-worlds interpretation of quantum mechanics but compatible with hidden-variable approaches, demonstrating its potential to revive objective classicality within a quantum framework.  This research contributes to our understanding of the intricate relationships between decoherence, classicality, realism, and macroscopy, offering a comprehensive perspective on overcoming the quantum-classical boundary.  We further explore the implications of this perspective on reconciling quantum mechanics with relativity and the emergence of macroscopic quantum coherence in complex systems, as well as its applications in quantum optics, condense matter physics, and cosmology.  This comprehensive perspective on decoherence and classicality is found to be fundamental to developing a coherent quantum theory that extends beyond the standard Copenhagen approach, allowing for a more nuanced understanding of quantum phenomena and the development of novel quantum theories.  The paper concludes by outlining possible directions for advancing this perspective through theoretical advancements, experimental investigations, and the development of new open quantum systems techniques.  This comprehensive research on the origins of classicality within a quantum framework is intended to contribute significantly to our understanding of a fundamental phenomenon and may further pave the way for novel quantum theories and applications. As the wiretap channel is composed of multiple identical and independent sub-channels, we propose a scheme to encrypt each sub-channel individually. By applying the most secure coding technique to each sub-channel, we derive the overall wiretap channel's secrecy rate. Furthermore, due to the non-adaptive eavesdropping strategy, we can treat each sub-channel's error-correction code as if it were subject to the Hamming bound. By doing so, we obtain a closed-form expression for the maximum average error probability of each sub-channel. As a result, we can further optimize the encryption scheme to meet a predetermined error probability standard. Ultimately, by combining this optimized scheme with the most secure coding technique, we obtain the highest possible secrecy rate for the Erreur Correcte de Hamming model. Moreover, we demonstrate that this highest possible secrecy rate approaches the half-logarithm of the model's size as the size increases. Additionally, we observe that this highest possible secrecy rate can be approximated using the Gaussian distribution for large sizes. Finally, we conclude that this highest possible secrecy rate can be achieved through a binary coherent state quantum model with a similar statistics.  This research contributes to our understanding of fundamental secrecy rate limits in the Erreur Correcte de Hamming model. Despite the significance of this desire, research on the effectiveness of batched dynamic GNNs and their optimization remains limited.  To fill this knowledge gap, we conducted extensive experiments on both dynamic GNNs and their optimization algorithms, which yielded notable findings.  Initially, we investigated the performance of GDNBT (a recently proposed dynamic GNN model) and discovered that simply adding deleted edges back into the dynamic graph prior to computation as described in the original GDNBT research is ineffective.  Furthermore, we found that incorporating deleted edges results in the model learning unnecessary information that may even be detrimental.  To address this issue, we proposed an optimized variant of the GDNBT model called OLGDNBT, which involves adding deleted edges back into the dynamic graph after computation, along with another variant called TLGDNBT, which involves adding deleted edges back into the time-evolving graph structure after computation. Ultimately, we contributed our findings along with two new optimization algorithms (AGD and TFGD) to the body of knowledge, which are suitable for the proposed optimized models and yielded the best results in all experiments. of the heavy electron material UCoMd5, which was found to exhibit a long-wavelength magnetic instability at a critical wavevector of approximately 0.75 r.l.u. in the [110] direction. This instability is believed to stem from the strong hybridization between 5f electrons and the nearly full 4f shell of the lanthanide sublattice. Theoretical calculations using a local density approximation were conducted to analyze the underlying causes of this phenomenon. The results indicate that the primary factor contributing to the instability is the noncollinear magnetic arrangement itself, which breaks exchange integrals and facilitates the long-wavelength instability. Additionally, the first-order magnetic transition at 2.4 K is thought to be linked to this instability. The noncollinear structure may be viewed as a precursor to a more complex magnetic ground state, which could involve long-range magnetic ordering along the [110] direction. The nonlocal RKKY interactions are found to play a crucial role in shaping the magnetic properties of UCoMd5, differing significantly from the local approximation. The data obtained from SQUID magnetometry, neutron scattering, and x-ray resonant scattering are in agreement with these theoretical findings, confirming the noncollinear nature of the magnetic structure. The results obtained from the band structure calculations are also validated by x-ray photoemission spectroscopy measurements. The data obtained from specific heat measurements indicate that the heavy fermion behavior is preserved within the noncollinear magnetic phase. The properties of UCoMd5 provide valuable insights into the complex relationships between 4f and 5f electrons, as well as the underlying mechanisms driving noncollinear magnetic ordering in heavy electron compounds. We investigated the connection between the disc cavity's location and the properties of a starburst, using a sample of 72 AGNs with optical spectra, and 23 of these with high-quality radio data. This research provides evidence that a starburst is the primary cause of the disc cavity observed in some AGNs.  Based on this findings, we propose a model in which molecular gas, heated by the starburst, produces X-rays that clear the disc cavity. the development of numerical methods for resolving the nonlinear dynamics of coupled oscillators in the context of van der Waals systems. As a key component of these systems, a critical role is played by the quantum fluctuations affecting the transition energies. Despite the importance of accurate information about oscillator frequencies, even tiny changes in these frequencies can significantly impact the behavior of nonlinear dynamics. To effectively analyze the nonlinear dynamics of these oscillators, we advocate the use of sophisticated numerical methods that are capable of resolving very small frequency differences. Beginning with an overview of the model and relevant conservation laws, we delibly outline the strategy for resolving the spectrum of the resulting complex dynamical system. A key point is the appropriate choice of the oscillator frequency scale, which is integral to resolving the spectrum. By employing the Laguerre polynomial basis, we demonstrate the efficiency of the numerical methods in resolving the ring-shaped modes. Furthermore, we verify the accuracy of these methods by successfully resolving the doughnut-shaped mode, a more challenging scenario with a higher amplitude. As a testament to the power of these sophisticated numerical approaches, we are able to observe a novel phenomenon - the formation of a ring-shaped mode in the blue-shifted oscillator - surpassing the curve of the normal-mode spectrum. Finally, we validate the adequacy of these methods by successfully resolving the crescent-shaped mode with a higher amplitude, all in the context of a specific example with fixed values. As a means of exploring the relationship between normal-mode spectrum curves, we include a diagram illustrating how a slight shift in the blue-edge frequency can lead to a crescent-shaped mode with a lower amplitude. As a further example, we present a scenario with a higher amplitude, demonstrating how a minor shift in the blue-edge frequency is necessary to transform the ring-shaped mode into a doughnut-shaped mode with a higher amplitude. As a whole, this research contributes to our understanding of the nonlinear dynamics of coupled van der Waals oscillators, offering a wealth of information for the development of theoretical models, particularly in the characterization of micraculeons, a type of exciton-polariton with a small mass. Additionally, this study extends our knowledge of the nonlinear behavior of ring-shaped modes in the context of cavity polaritons, paving the way for its application in the control of nonlinear effects in exciton-polariton systems.  This manuscript is a comprehensive review of numerical methods for resolving the nonlinear dynamics of coupled oscillators in van der Waals systems, focusing on the implementation of sophisticated numerical approaches to resolve very small frequency differences. 2 transmission has been a subject of considerable debate, with some research suggesting that the virus may be airborne, despite initial claims that it primarily spreads through contact with contaminated surfaces.  Using detailed atomic-level simulations, we investigated the stability of the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein in air, focusing on factors that influence its stability and the potential for transmission.  Our results indicate that the virus's low stability in aerosols is not inherent, as the spike protein's stability is preserved when bound to angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2), a key receptor for SARS-CoV-2.  However, once the virus comes into contact with dry air, the spike protein degrades rapidly, which should significantly impede transmission through aerosols.  On the other hand, the virus's stability is maintained when bound to ACE2 or covered by saliva/mucus, facilitating contact transmission.  Our findings provide a molecular explanation for the observed patterns of SARS-CoV-2 transmission and suggest that the primary modes of infection are close contact with an infected individual or contaminated surface, contradicting the possibility of airborne transmission in typical environments.  However, we note that transmission may occur in isolated cases where the virus is highly concentrated in aerosols, such as during intense singing or other loud activities that produce large amounts of saliva/mucus droplets.  Ultimately, our research highlights the importance of accurate information about virus transmission mechanisms and encourages policymakers to rely on scientifically validated data when developing infection control strategies.  Our simulations using molecular dynamics also contribute to a broader understanding of protein stability and can be applied to similar analyses of other biological systems.  Additionally, our code and data are available for other research groups to use and build upon, potentially leading to new discoveries about SARS-CoV-2 and other coronaviruses.  Furthermore, our findings align with existing research on the stability of coronaviruses in aerosols and offer a molecular explanation for the observed patterns of SARS-CoV-2 transmission.  Our results should be useful in informing policy decisions about room ventilation requirements for areas where the virus is present, as well as guiding research into the development of effective anti-SARS-CoV-2 proteins and vaccines. neural network architectures has led to a growing interest in parallelizing computation across layers, a technique known as layer-wise parallelization.  As the number of layers in a neural network continues to grow, optimizing the performance of layer-wise parallelization is increasingly important.  To achieve high performance, researchers have explored various strategies for managing memory and executing parallelized layers, including hardware-specific optimizations and parallel computing frameworks.  Despite these efforts, the current state of layer-wise parallelization remains limited by a fundamental constraint, a constraint that is not inherently performance-related but rather an inherent property of the current architecture.  The purpose of this research is to eliminate this inherent limitation and explore alternative approaches to parallelizing computation across layers.  Our investigation reveals that the classic, straightforward method of replicating hardware resources across layers yields negligible performance gains.  As a more effective alternative, we propose a design that places hardware resources between layers, a design known as transverse parallelization.  Our research demonstrates that transverse parallelization can significantly improve performance by offering multiple options for arranging hardware resources in a three-dimensional network topology.  Our findings show that a simple shape with a high aspect ratio is not necessarily the most efficient option, discounting regular rectangular shapes that can be divided into squares.  Instead, we identify the optimal transverse parallelization architectures as a collection of square areas in a one-dimensional array, a pattern known as a checkerboard or golf ball shape, a pattern that offers the highest possible throughput of 768 million layers per second on a single ASIC device with a small footprint of 0.153 mm^2.  Our research further explores the possibility of embedding transverse parallelization within existing hardware frameworks, demonstrating the feasibility of implementing transverse parallelization within a single ASIC device, a co-processor, and a GPU.  Our research contributes to our understanding of the theoretical limits of layer-wise parallelization, offering multiple options for arranging hardware resources, which can be applied to various neural network architectures, which we demonstrate through a range of case studies, including ResNets, ChannelNet, and ShiftNet.  Our research also derives mathematical formulas to evaluate the performance of transverse parallelization architectures in hardware, which can be used to design customized hardware devices for specific neural network architectures. This phenomenon was initially identified within the group of automorphisms of the unit circle, and a more general account was then provided within the symplectic group Sp(2n). This paper delves into the underlying reasons for this phenomenon, focusing on a key aspect: the failure to achieve equalities in the inequalities defining the operator norms of these composition operators. While most research on electron and ion instabilities in magnetized plasmas linearizes growth rate calculations, the Kelvin-Helmholtz instability, occurring at high beta values, might behave nonlinearly due to weak growth rates and significant plasma flow velocities.  To better understand the nonlinear behavior of the Kelvin-Helmholtz instability in a burnings plasma scenario, we conduct a comprehensive analysis of its growth rates and evolution, focusing on a realistic model with variable anisotropy.  Initially, we observe that even slight anisotropy can significantly impact instability growth rates, shifting the instability to higher k values in a more anisotropic environment.  As beta value increases, so does the nonlinear growth rate, although the overall growth rate decreases.  To further explore nonlinear effects, we compare growth rates obtained through linear and nonlinear theory, finding that the nonlinear approach yields higher growth rates, especially at higher beta values and greater anisotropy levels.  Finally, we analyze the critical balance condition, finding that the most unstable wavelength satisfies a nonlinear scaling relationship, with both k and gamma~beta**(-0.5).  In a standard algebraic decay model, we find that the nonlinear growth rate is directly proportional to the product of the instability wavelength and the cross-field electron drift velocity.  Additionally, we conduct a particle simulation of the Kelvin-Helmholtz instability in a burning plasma scenario, observing that despite low growth rates, the instability can still lead to significant electron heating, aligning with nonlinear theory expectations.  Ultimately, this research demonstrates that the Kelvin-Helmholtz instability in a burning plasma scenario exhibits nonlinear growth characteristics, which can result in substantial electron heating, potentially affecting algebraic decay instability growth rates and overall instability behavior.  This study's findings are crucial for developing a comprehensive understanding of instability dynamics in a burning plasma scenario, which is essential for advancing magnetized plasma stability research.  Additionally, this research's outcomes can be applied to other anisotropic instability scenarios, such as the ring shear instability and the oblique tearing mode.  Furthermore, this study's methodology can be used to investigate other nonlinear growth rate effects in plasma instability scenarios. Although extensive research has been conducted on this topic, there's a significant gap in existing studies regarding the dynamic aspect of job arrivals and machine breakdowns.  To address this gap, this research proposes a novel, two-stage bilevel metaheuristic to solve the DJSSP with uncertain job arrivals and machine failures, aiming to minimize total completion time and maximize system throughput.  The first stage uses the Dynamic Largest Weighted Degree (DLWD) algorithm to solve a static version of the problem, while the second stage employs a hybrid genetic algorithm to explore the dynamic scenario.  To further enhance solution accuracy, a peak tabu search is integrated into the genetic algorithm.  Additionally, a parallel computing approach is employed to speed up the solution process.  To evaluate the proposed method, we conducted comprehensive simulations using large-scale instances derived from the static job-shop scheduling problem, yielding promising results.  The proposed approach demonstrates a significant improvement in total completion time compared to existing methods, as well as a notable increase in system throughput.  Furthermore, the research investigates the structural characteristics of the DJSSP in response to varying parameters of job arrivals and machine failures, revealing a proportional relationship between total completion time and the square root of the number of job arrivals.  Finally, we demonstrate the applicability of the proposed model to various real-world scenarios, including a manufacturing company, a hospital, and a call center, showcasing its potential to contribute significantly to system optimization.  The proposed two-stage bilevel metaheuristic provides a versatile framework for solving the DJSSP, along with a suite of algorithms and strategies that can be adapted to address various variations of the problem and its byproducts, opening up possibilities for future research. This paper reviews the available evidence on the effectiveness of using plain-language messages and statistical models in sugar intake reduction, with a focus on its impact evaluation.  We examined both the theoretical basis for these interventions and the empirical studies that have tested their effectiveness, drawing on a broad range of nutritional and health outcomes.  We also explored the methodological aspects of conducting and reporting impact evaluations, including the importance of accounting for confounding variables, the advantages of using within-group comparisons, and the value of conducting sensitivity analyses.  Ultimately, our research findings suggest that both plain-language messages and statistical models have a positive impact on reducing sugar intake, although the extent of this effect varies based on factors like population demographics and the specific outcome being measured.  We believe that combining these interventions with established nutritional guidelines could lead to significant sugar intake reductions, potentially as much as 0.5 to 1.5 teaspoons per day.  We also emphasize the need for more studies on the effectiveness of these interventions, particularly among underrepresented populations, in order to further refine our understanding of their impact and its possible variations.  Additionally, we propose a number of recommendations for both researchers and policymakers on how to optimize the effectiveness of sugar intake reduction initiatives by utilizing plain-language messages and statistical models, along with a call for a more comprehensive evaluation of the factors influencing sugar intake.  We believe that a better understanding of these influences could lead to a more targeted and efficient reduction of sugar intake at the population level.  We have made our code available online to facilitate the replication of our results and the implementation of future studies.  We hope that our research will contribute to a more informed public health response to the issue of excessive sugar consumption. To better understand this connection, we propose an observational campaign that would utilize the D-alpha line, in conjunction with other key magnetic diagnosis methods such as spectropolarimetry and magnetoseismology, to study and map magnetic inclination and strength during periodic magnetic reconnection events. By applying these distinct observations and theoretical models, we aim to establish a direct link between D-alpha line emission and magnetic parameters, facilitating the development of efficient, possibly non-local, mechanisms for generating and heating chromospheric plasma. By achieving this goal, it will be possible to improve current numerical models and MHD simulations, ultimately contributing to a more comprehensive understanding of magnetic reconnection's effects on solar and stellar atmospheres. Given the economic incentives driving market participation, we can analyze the strategic decisions made by generators regarding resource adequacy compensation and capacity market auctions.  Through a game-theoretic model, we explored the relationship between resource adequacy requirements, capacity market auctions, and spot market prices.  A key finding is that an equilibrium exists where generators may choose not to build capacity, despite resource adequacy requirements and positive economic conditions, leaving a need for more conservative reserve requirements.  Additionally, we discovered that a surge in demand for capacity leads to a decrease in spot market prices, and an increase in revenue for generators in a lower capacity demand bracket compared to a higher one.  These findings suggest that the current resource adequacy mechanism is not effective in ensuring generation capacity and can be improved by prioritizing resource adequacy through capacity auctions over spot market revenue, or by introducing a minimum capacity payment standard.  As this research utilized a simplified model, we acknowledge its limitations and aim to extend it in future studies.  Furthermore, we propose three alternative resource adequacy mechanisms on the German electricity market, which can be evaluated using the same theoretical framework, along with suggestions for regulators.  The first mechanism involves prioritizing resource adequacy through capacity auctions over spot market revenue, which can be implemented by modifying existing market rules.  The second mechanism involves introducing a minimum capacity payment standard, which can be achieved through regulatory decisions.  The third mechanism involves designing a two-dimensional capacity market auction, which requires technical developments but offers more beneficial payoffs for generators.  Case studies on a potential shortage and a surplus of capacity illustrate the effectiveness of these alternatives.  The first study shows that prioritizing resource adequacy through capacity auctions over spot market revenue leads to more generation capacity and higher payments compared to the current mechanism.  The second study demonstrates that introducing a minimum capacity payment standard of 50 euros/MW/day results in more generation capacity and higher payments compared to the current mechanism.  The third study shows that designing a two-dimensional capacity market auction with a high low-capacity auction price and a low high-capacity auction price leads to more generation capacity and higher payments compared to the current mechanism.  These alternative resource adequacy mechanisms can be evaluated further and combined with other existing mechanisms to optimize generation capacity on the German electricity market.  As this research offers new theoretical insights on the strategic behavior of generators regarding resource adequacy compensation and capacity market auctions, it contributes to the literature on the subject. Although it appears to be a minor adjustment, the implications of label smoothing are complex and far-reaching, affecting both the theory and the practice of classification models.  In this paper, we conduct a comprehensive exploration of the reasons behind label smoothing's popularity, analyzing its underlying motivations, examining its effects on both the model's performance and the information encoded in the models, and delving into the computational implications of applying the smooth entropy loss function.  Our in-depth investigation reveals that label smoothing is not simply a single, uniform treatment but can be viewed as a variety of distinct techniques, each with its own characteristics, necessitating a reevaluation of established theoretical insights.  Moreover, we identify a novel boundary in the information-theoretic framework that provides a precise explanation for the optimal label smoothing technique, which we refer to as squared-label smoothing.  Through a series of theoretical analyses, we demonstrate that squared-label smoothing offers improved performance over traditional label smoothing, verifying this finding with numerous empirical experiments across a range of classification models and datasets.  One of the most intriguing aspects of our research is the discovery that squared-label smoothing corresponds to a specific regularization approach that we call between-class loss, which is distinct from other established loss functions.  Our research contributes substantially to the existing body of knowledge by presenting a coherent, unified framework that integrates classification models, loss functions, and data distributions, which we believe will be highly influential in the development of future loss function designs.  Furthermore, we demonstrate that our proposed framework is applicable to a wide range of loss function designs, including but not limited to loss functions that are based on entropy, mutual information, and cross-entropy, which we verify through a series of theoretical derivations and empirical experiments.  Our research findings provide a strong foundation for the development of loss function techniques that are tailored to various machine learning tasks, applications, and problems, which we aim to explore in our proposed future research directions. explosive vests in images obtained from drones poses a significant technical challenge, particularly when the context is not well-defined.  To investigate this challenge, we created a large dataset of images featuring concealed explosives and weapons obtained from Google searches, which is unusual and difficult to classify.  Our research team trained a convolutional neural network on this uncurated data, which resulted in a detection accuracy of 90% for universally recognized explosives and 80% for weapons, although the system failed to detect the most concealed items.  However, when we incorporated context obtained from Google, in the form of descriptions and keywords, into the image, the detection rate more than doubled for both categories, demonstrating the importance of context in anomaly detection.  We also experimented with incorporating context obtained from typical scenarios where drones are used, which yielded even better results, indicating that the system learns unnecessary preferences for Western images and clothing.  As a remedy, we developed a fairness metric to evaluate the bias of the network and a technique to eliminate it, which was successful in eliminating context obtained from descriptions but not from scenarios.  To further enhance the effectiveness of context, we designed a multi-component model that learns to weigh the importance of context, which outperformed a single-weight model and yielded overall high scores for morality, fairness, and accuracy.  Our research indicates that, despite the large volume of data, context remains crucial in anomaly detection and that incorporating external knowledge may obfuscate issues of data bias but is no substitute for solving them at their source.  Our findings have important implications for the development of systems that utilize context in anomaly detection, particularly in situations where data diversity is limited, and we propose several courses of action to eliminate context bias, including selecting more diverse data, reformulating descriptions, and adjusting algorithms.  Our research is available for replication, and our code and datasets can be found at https://github.com/ghiu1/ContextualAnomalyDetection. in 1979 as a measure of changes in the output of a program, and has since been studied in the context of sequential and parallel models of computation.  We explore here the notion of a more general metric, which we call a Dynamic Measure, applicable to a wide range of computational models and processes, including sequential, parallel, and probabilistic models, as well as models that generate infinite outputs.  We define three properties of a Dynamic Measure: (i) it should be a function of the output's structure rather than its sequence; (ii) it should be compositional, meaning it reflects the sum of changes in sub-processes; and (iii) it should be scalable, meaning it doubles with double-length inputs.  We further define three conditions for a Dynamic Measure to be considered a Dynamic Complexity, which involves growth rates and the logarithmic function.  We present three open problems at the end of the chapter, concerning the identification of applicable Dynamic Measures in the categories of sequential, parallel, and probabilistic models, as well as models that generate finite outputs.  We believe that a comprehensive understanding of Dynamic Measures will contribute significantly to our overall understanding of computational complexity, and may further have implications for theoretical computer science, mathematics, and philosophy.  This research paper is intended as a foundational document, with the aim of establishing a new area of investigation into the metrics of computational changes.  It is written in an accessible style, with the goal of appealing to a broad range of audiences, including researchers, students, and philosophers.  It is further hoped that a thorough exploration of Dynamic Measures will lead to novel insights into the fundamental nature of computation, as well as its boundaries, possibilities, and limitations.  As such, we have included a list of suggested readings at the end of the chapter, which is intended to provide a comprehensive introduction to the theoretical background of Dynamic Measures.  We have further made the decision to release the paper under an open-access license, in order to facilitate the creation of a dedicated website for the purpose of community engagement, which will be accompanied by a series of companion documents that will be made available on the arXiv preprint server.
