a class of astronomical events involving enormous energy releases, often associated with distant starburst galaxies or with the explosion of massive stars.  While the majority of GRBs fit into one of these two categories, a small subset known as Long Duration GRBs with large energy releases (LGRBs) exhibit peculiar characteristics that defy their established theories.  These unusual features include their remarkable distances and the presence of heavy elements, which contradict the standard models of GRB formation through massive star collapse and radioactivity-driven explosions.  A new possibility has emerged to explain these unusual LGRBs, involving an explosive event that occurs when a massive star surges beyond a critical limit, injecting heavy elements into the gas and driving the burst.  This new theory aligns with observations of a remarkable GRB 060614, a repeat event that occurred in a distant galaxy with a low metallicity, and a similar GRB 161219B, which occurred in a gas rich with heavy elements and showed signs of a massive star explosion.  These findings suggest that unusual LGRBs originate from the explosive events that mark the final stages of massive star collapse, offering a new understanding of these enigmatic events and their place within the broader context of astrophysical phenomena.  This new understanding also presents opportunities for studying the formation of heavy elements in the universe and the properties of massive stars through further research into these unusual LGRBs.  Additionally, this theory may be relevant to other extreme astrophysical events such as supernovae and hypernovae, providing a unified framework for their explanation.  This perspective article aims to outline the emerging picture of unusual LGRBs, explore their implications, and identify areas for future study.  It is proposed that a collaborative effort be made to develop a comprehensive model of these events through a combination of observational and theoretical studies.  This model can be utilized to search for unusual LGRBs, analyze their characteristics, and investigate the formation of heavy elements in the universe.  This new area of research has the potential to contribute significantly to our understanding of extreme astrophysical phenomena and the formation of heavy elements in the universe.  This research is particularly relevant to the upcoming generation of high-energy gamma-ray observatories such as the Gamma-ray Transient Monitor and the Advanced Telescope for X-rays 2--10 keV.  It is also anticipated that a similar population of unusual LGRBs may be discovered through the survey of nearby starburst galaxies with the Square Kilometre Array and the next generation of high-energy gamma-ray observatories.

Active learning is a popular technique for both machine learning model improvement and data labeling, with the most uncertain samples typically presented to an informant for labeling. Since the majority of the strongest gamma-ray bursts occur in distant starforming galaxies, we anticipate that the most potent bursts will be discovered in the LVHalpha survey, which is predicted to uncover numerous strong GRB aftermaths, along with a possible historic discovery of a blastwave influenced by a nearby historic burst, GRB 021213. The LVHalpha survey's initial results have already led to the discovery of multiple strong gamma-ray burst aftermaths, including the largest blastwave observed to date, GRB 054Bb, and a possible historic blastwave influenced by a nearby historic burst, GRB 021213. Additionally, existing research may not accurately reflect the prevalence of substandard/falsified medical products in these areas due to various methodological limitations. This new approach extends the traditional linear state-space formulation to a higher-dimensional space, allowing for easier control design through the use of linear matrix inequalities.  A key advantage of this method is that it can improve control design in systems prone to saturation, as well as those with actuator delays, without the need for modeling these limitations accurately.  Without sacrificing generality, we utilize a specific second-order system with delayed actuation as a representative example, demonstrating how the new approach leads to more efficient control design compared to the traditional method.  Furthermore, we provide a straightforward way to design a boundary control layer around the desired trajectory, which is critical for avoiding trajectory-specific oscillations in systems with delayed actuation.  A key aspect of this design is the inclusion of a condition to minimize the variance of the new state variable, which is essential for eliminating boundary oscillations in an open-loop fashion.  To validate this new approach, we apply it to a sample system and confirm that it is feasible to design a control strategy that results in a smooth, parabolic boundary around a desired circular trajectory, even in the presence of disturbances.  As a further test, we derive a control scheme for a second-order mass-spring-damper system with delayed actuation that is subject to a predefined circular boundary, demonstrating its effectiveness in suppressing oscillations and removing distortion from a distorted circular trajectory with a central hole.  In both cases, the proposed control strategy proves to be more efficient than the traditional one, which fails to produce a smooth boundary in both instances.  Additionally, we include a comprehensive analysis of the mathematical stability properties of the new control approach, demonstrating that it leads to a properly stable closed-loop system even in the presence of disturbances. One particular pattern that stands out is the one where activity is concentrated in a single location, while remaining dormant at all other sites. This specific pattern is considered the most prominent or the "winning" pattern. The underlying reasons for the formation of this pattern can be attributed to the competition among various patterns for limited resources, in much the same way that fair elections dictate a single winner. Furthermore, the margin by which the winning pattern prevails over the others is analogous to the majority vote it receives. This distinct approach to understanding how patterns emerge through the competition for resources is known as a "voting" model. It has been demonstrated that globally coupled oscillators operating under the Oswald condition will invariably produce the winning pattern as the primary outcome. What remains unclear is how the spread of activated areas in the winning pattern is determined. It is essential to note that the spread of areas with significant influence mirrors the spread of areas with significant activity in the winning pattern. On the other hand, areas with little to no influence will correspond to areas with little to no activity. Although oxide-based memristors have been extensively studied, their complexity and the requirements for high temperature processing hinder their suitability for integrating nanoscale devices within neural networks.  In contrast, organic-based memristors offer a more feasible option for integrating devices within neural networks due to their simplicity and compatibility with flexible substrates. Despite the straightforward essence of graph editing sequences, evaluating their equivalence is notoriously difficult as even determining the equivalence of two single editing steps within a sequence remains a challenging task. This proof's key step involves showing that every positive even integer can be expressed as the sum of three cubes of integers modulo some power of 2. Rubinstein developed a method for computing the number of rational points on a curve over a finite field, and they also showed that this number can be found using the Euclidean algorithm. Recently, Scheidt provided an alternative approach based on the extended Euclidean algorithm and its inversion, and he also extended the method to include curves defined over other fields. Here, we present a simplified version of their algorithm and extend it in three ways: (1) we show that the algorithm can be described using only basic operations; (2) we demonstrate that the algorithm's inversion step is unnecessary; (3) we extend the algorithm to include curves defined over fields with large cardinality. Additionally, we present a theoretical time complexity of the algorithm for curves defined over infinite fields, and we also provide a concise description of the algorithm suitable for implementation. As an example, we outline a possible implementation of the algorithm using Python's built-in functions, and we also describe a possible optimization using a modular extended Euclidean algorithm. Finally, we discuss possible future directions of the research.  This paper is a compilation of results from the following three papers: "Counting Rational Points on Curves over the reals" by Speyer and Rubinstein, "Counting Points on Curves over Finite Fields" by Scheidt, "A Point Counting Algorithm for Curves over Unbounded Fields" by Gruenbacher and Scheidt, and "Point Counting on Curves over the reals" by Gruenbacher.  This paper is aimed at mathematicians who work with point counting algorithms and researchers in the field of algebraic geometry.
